subject: political-science
part: Part III · The European Union as a Political System
readings: Bulmer, Parker, Bache, George & Burns (2020) ch. 19, "The Single Market" · Jensen & Nedergaard (2012), "From 'Frankenstein' to 'toothless vampire'?"

cards.front: What is a **single market**?
cards.back: A market where **goods, services, capital and people** move freely, so that crossing a national border adds no extra cost to economic activity.

cards.front: What is the difference between a **free trade area**, a **customs union**, and a **single market**?
cards.back:
1) **Free trade area**: members drop tariffs among themselves but keep their own external tariffs.
2) **Customs union**: a free trade area plus a **common external tariff**.
3) **Single market**: a customs union plus removal of **non tariff barriers** and the four freedoms.

cards.front: Name the concept: national rules, product standards, licences and admin requirements that block trade even after tariffs and quotas are gone.
cards.back: **Non tariff barriers (NTBs).** They are much harder to remove than tariffs, so they are the real work of the single market.

cards.front: What are the **three layers of trade barrier**, from easiest to hardest to remove?
cards.back: 1) **Tariffs** (largely removed). 2) **Quantitative restrictions / quotas** (prohibited). 3) **Non tariff barriers** (much harder, the real work).
cards.hint: Tariffs, quotas, then the hard layer.

cards.front: Name the **four freedoms** of the single market.
cards.back: Free movement of 1) **goods**, 2) **services**, 3) **capital**, and 4) **people / labour**.

cards.front: Which of the four freedoms is **furthest along** and acts as the model for the whole market?
cards.back: **Free movement of goods.** It was solved by the "new approach": mutual recognition by default plus minimum EU harmonization only on health and safety.
cards.hint: You can ship it in a box.

cards.front: How does the **"new approach" to standards** free the movement of goods without harmonizing every rule (ending in the **CE mark**)?
cards.back:
1) Default rule is **mutual recognition**: a product lawfully sold in one state is legal in all.
2) Exception is **health and safety**: the EU sets minimum standards via **CEN / CENELEC**.
3) A product meeting them earns the **"CE" mark** and cannot be barred anywhere.
cards.hint: Mutual recognition plus minimum health and safety.

cards.front: The 1985 White Paper split the barriers to **goods** into which three kinds?
cards.back: 1) **Physical** (border checks). 2) **Fiscal** (VAT and excise, only partly done). 3) **Technical** (product standards, the hard one).

cards.front: In free movement of **persons**, beyond workers, to whom were residence rights extended?
cards.back: To the **economically inactive**: students, the retired and the unemployed, with non discrimination in social and welfare benefits.

cards.front: What is the **main barrier** to real labour mobility in the EU?
cards.back: **Non recognition of professional and educational qualifications**: a nurse or architect qualified in one state may not be recognized in another.

cards.front: Which freedom "had already started to disappear" as a barrier and was largely freed early by the White Paper?
cards.back: **Free movement of capital.** The White Paper freed cross border securities, loans and access to foreign stock exchanges.

cards.front: What is the **unfinished business** of capital integration?
cards.back: Integrating capital **markets**: the **Financial Services Action Plan (1999)** and, under Juncker, the **Capital Markets Union** to channel savings into SMEs.

cards.front: Why are **services** so much harder to integrate than goods?
cards.back: Because a service is often **inseparable from the person or organization providing it**: you cannot ship it in a box. Providing it across a border needs people, professional qualifications, local licences, establishment abroad and dealing with national regulators, plus more information asymmetry and trust. By 2005 only about 20% of services were traded across borders.

cards.front: The EU liberalized services sector by sector. Why was **telecoms** easier than **energy**?
cards.back:
1) **Telecoms**: relatively successful, helped by US deregulation pressure and business lobbying.
2) **Energy**: harder, blocked by the "public service argument", French defence of **EdF / Gaz de France** and union job fears.
Both were prised open sector by sector over national monopoly resistance.
cards.hint: One had US pressure behind it.

cards.front: What is the difference between **negative** and **positive** integration, and who is the chief agent of each?
cards.back:
1) **Negative integration**: remove barriers, prohibit discrimination, strike down national rules. Chief agent: the **CJEU**.
2) **Positive integration**: create common EU rules (harmonization). Chief agents: **Commission, Council and EP**.
The EU uses both.

cards.front: What did the CJEU decide in ***Cassis de Dijon* (1979)**, and what principle did it establish?
cards.back: Germany blocked a French blackcurrant liqueur for failing its minimum alcohol rule. The CJEU **struck the barrier down** and established **mutual recognition**: a product lawfully marketed in one member state should generally be allowed onto another's market. It integrated through law, with no new legislation.

cards.front: Name the principle: a product lawfully sold in one member state may generally be sold in all of them.
cards.back: **Mutual recognition.** It is the engine of negative integration: the Court removes a barrier without any new legislation.

cards.front: What is the difference between **harmonization** and **mutual recognition**, with a pro and con of each?
cards.back:
1) **Harmonization**: replace national rules with common EU rules. Pro: a level playing field. Con: slow and politically hard.
2) **Mutual recognition**: keep national rules but each state recognizes the other's. Pro: fast, respects diversity. Con: fear of a "race to the bottom".

cards.front: What was **"Project 1992"** (the Cockfield White Paper)?
cards.back: The 1985 Delors Commission's **Cockfield White Paper**, listing about 279 measures to remove remaining barriers, with a hard deadline of 31 December 1992.

cards.front: Which 1987 treaty change made the 1992 relaunch **decidable**, and how?
cards.back: The **Single European Act (1987)**: it expanded **Qualified Majority Voting** for market laws, so single market measures could no longer be vetoed by one state.
cards.hint: QMV and the end of the veto.

cards.front: The market stalled through the 1970s ("eurosclerosis"). Why did the **1992 relaunch** finally deliver it?
cards.back:
It needed both an idea and a way to decide.
1) **The idea**: "Project 1992", the Cockfield White Paper listing about 279 measures with a 1992 deadline.
2) **The way to decide**: the Single European Act's expanded **QMV**, removing the national veto.
The market needed an economic plan and a way to make collective decisions.
cards.hint: An idea plus a way to decide.

cards.front: A Polish firm wins a temporary job in Denmark. Under the **country of origin** vs **host country** principle, whose rules apply and what is the trade off?
cards.back:
1) **Country of origin (home country)**: the firm uses its own Polish rules. Frictionless, but risks a "race to the bottom".
2) **Host country**: the firm must meet Denmark's rules. Protects standards, but fragments the market again.
The master question: which country should regulate cross border activity?
cards.hint: Frictionless but risky vs protective but fragmenting.

cards.front: Who proposed the 2004 **Services Directive**, and what was its explosive core principle?
cards.back: Commissioner **Frits Bolkestein**. Its core was the **country of origin principle**: firms could provide services abroad under their home country rules, a Cassis style move for services.

cards.front: Trace the Services Directive from **"Frankenstein" to "toothless vampire"**.
cards.back:
1) **Proposal (2004)**: Bolkestein's country of origin directive.
2) **Explosion**: fear of "social dumping" after the 2004 enlargement (the "Polish plumber", Laval); unions mobilized; France called it the "Frankenstein directive".
3) **Dilution (2006)**: country of origin removed, host country labour law preserved, whole sectors excluded, a screening system added.

cards.front: What replaced the country of origin principle in the final Services Directive?
cards.back: A vaguer **"freedom to provide services"** clause, leaving much room for later **CJEU** interpretation; host country labour law was preserved.

cards.front: What overall framework do **Jensen & Nedergaard** use to explain the watering down of the Services Directive?
cards.back: **Actor centred rational choice institutionalism.** The European Parliament seemed decisive, but the real drivers were bargaining and interests.

cards.front: In Jensen & Nedergaard, how did the German **grand coalition** shape the outcome?
cards.back: The new **CDU/CSU and SPD coalition (November 2005)** used ties to both big EP groups (EPP and PES) to broker a lowest common denominator text.

cards.front: Using **Olson's** logic, why did unions beat consumers over the Services Directive?
cards.back: **Unions had concentrated costs**, so they mobilized; **consumers had diffuse gains**, so they did not organize. States with the most barriers opposed the most.

cards.front: How does **Putnam's** two level games logic explain the Services Directive bargain?
cards.back: France and Germany bargained by pointing to **small domestic win sets** (referendum pressure). The deal was struck "in the shadow of the vote", a credible blocking minority.
cards.hint: In the shadow of the vote.

cards.front: Why did central and eastern European states accept the diluted Services Directive?
cards.back: They had **large win sets** (any improvement beat the status quo), so they took the low denominator, winning the **screening system** as a bargaining chip.

cards.front: Name the fear: firms from low wage states undercutting high wage states by importing their cheaper home rules.
cards.back: **Social dumping.** Its folk devil was the French "Polish plumber"; the fear grew after the 2004 eastern enlargement and helped sink the 2005 Constitution referendums.

cards.front: What is a **posted worker**?
cards.back: An employee **temporarily sent** by an employer to another EU member state to provide a service.

cards.front: Why does a single **posting** create a governance knot?
cards.back: One posting tangles three rule systems at once: 1) the **home country employment relationship**, 2) the **host country workplace**, and 3) **EU free movement rules**. Which rules apply, and who enforces them, stays unresolved.

cards.front: What did the CJEU decide in the **Laval / Vaxholm case (2007)**, and why was it a shock?
cards.back: A Latvian firm renovated a Swedish school using Latvian workers on Latvian pay; Swedish unions blockaded it. The CJEU sided largely with the firm's **freedom to provide services** over collective action. It shocked Nordic wage setting, which relies on collective bargaining, not statutory minimum wages.
cards.hint: Freedom to provide services beat the unions.

cards.front: Which thesis do **Laval and Viking (2007)** most sharply support?
cards.back: **Scharpf's**: negative integration beats positive. The Court can strike down national social protections faster than the EU can legislate replacements.

cards.front: How did the EU shift posting rules from **"market opening" to "fair mobility"**?
cards.back: 1) **Posting of Workers Directive (1996)** → 2) **Enforcement Directive (2014)** → 3) **2018 revision** strengthening host country pay ("equal pay for equal work in the same place") and distinguishing short term from long term postings.

cards.front: How does an integrated market change what a national government can decide, **before** vs **after**?
cards.back:
**Before**: it could largely decide who enters the market, which standards apply, which firms get support and which services are protected.
**After**: those choices are constrained by EU free movement rules, competition rules, common standards and CJEU case law.
The state turns from **gatekeeper** into **rule taker**.

cards.front: In one phrase, how does the single market change the state's role?
cards.back: From **gatekeeper** to **rule taker**: the state does not disappear but operates inside EU constraints.

cards.front: How has the single market evolved from the eurozone crisis **into the digital age**?
cards.back: After 2009 falling intra EU trade revived economic nationalism → the **Monti report (2010)** → **Single Market Act I (2011) and II (2012)**. Juncker added the **Capital Markets Union** and the **Digital Single Market** (roaming charges abolished 2017). Today the **DMA**, **DSA** and **AI Act** tackle platforms and data.
cards.hint: Monti, Single Market Acts, digital acts.

cards.front: What is the most tangible thing the **Digital Single Market** delivered for ordinary citizens?
cards.back: The **abolition of mobile roaming charges in 2017**.

cards.front: What is **Majone's** view of the single market?
cards.back: The SEM makes the EU a **"regulatory state"**. Delegating regulation to non majoritarian institutions maximizes efficiency; on this **output legitimacy** view there is no democratic deficit.

cards.front: What is **Scharpf's** "structural asymmetry" thesis?
cards.back: **Market making** (negative integration) races ahead while **market correcting** rules ("Social Europe") lag: the CJEU strikes down social protections faster than the EU can legislate them.

cards.front: What is the **critical political economy** critique of the single market (Scharpf, Cafruny & Ryner, van Apeldoorn)?
cards.back: The SEM embeds a US led **neoliberal turn**: privatization, welfare retrenchment and liberalized corporate governance, often at business's bidding (the **ERT**), eroding Europe's social models.

cards.front: What is **Hay and Wincott's** constructivist middle position?
cards.back: Both sides overstate structural imperatives. The market is **not fully depoliticized**: it is contestable, some CJEU rulings protected national prerogatives, and welfare capitalist diversity persists.

cards.front: What does **postfunctionalism** add to the neoliberalism debate?
cards.back: **Popular dissatisfaction** with the EU can act as a brake on further market integration. In the UK "Lexiteers" made a left wing case for Brexit.

cards.front: Apply **LI** vs **neofunctionalism** to Project 1992, Cassis, and the Services Directive.
cards.back:
**LI** reads it as states pursuing interests; **neofunctionalism** as supranational actors pushing.
1) **Project 1992**: LI sees converging preferences and bargaining; neofunctionalism sees Commission entrepreneurship (Delors, ERT).
2) **Cassis**: LI, states built the legal frame; neofunctionalism, the CJEU drives integration.
3) **Services Directive**: LI, a German brokered bargain; neofunctionalism, supranational ambition meeting resistance.
cards.hint: States bargaining vs Commission and Court pushing.

cards.front: Big picture: is the single market **economics or politics**, and does any one integration theory win?
cards.back: The **red thread**: the single market is an institutional and political project, not an automatic economic one; it develops through bargaining and changes the state from gatekeeper to rule taker. **On theory no single one wins**: states set the frame, but courts, the Commission and institutional momentum keep pushing it further than any single bargain intended.

cards.front: How does **Bulmer map** the integration theories onto the single market's phases?
cards.back:
1) The **original common market** fits **LI**.
2) The **1960 acceleration** looked **neofunctionalist**.
3) The **1992 relaunch** is genuinely contested (Delors/ERT vs Moravcsik).
4) The **momentum after 1992** fits **historical institutionalism**: the SEA changed the rules and the CJEU entrenched free market readings.
